subject: Career
title: Gaslighting at Work
description: A quick, practical guide to Gaslighting at Work.

hook.text: 'That's not what I said.' But it is. You have the email. Workplace gaslighting makes you doubt your own reality.

buildup.text: Gaslighting is a manipulation tactic that makes the target question their memory, perception, or sanity.

discovery.text: It's subtle: denying events, trivializing feelings, shifting blame. Over time, victims lose confidence in their own judgment.

twist.text: Gaslighters often target high performers — people whose competence threatens them.

climax.text: The antidote: document everything in writing. Trust the paper trail over the gaslighter's version.

punchline.text: If someone makes you doubt your own receipts, trust the receipts.

quiz.question: What is workplace gaslighting?
options: Manipulation that makes you doubt your own memory and perception

details.summary: Workplace gaslighting involves persistent manipulation that makes you doubt your own perceptions, memories, and competence. It is a form of psychological abuse that can be perpetrated by managers, peers, or organizational culture itself.
details.whyItMatters: Gaslighting is among the most damaging workplace behaviors because it erodes your confidence and self-trust. Recognizing it early prevents lasting psychological harm.
takeaways: Common signs include being told events did not happen as you remember
Document interactions in writing to create an objective record
Seek external validation from trusted people outside the situation

faq.question: How can you tell the difference between gaslighting and genuine disagreement?
faq.answer: Gaslighting involves a pattern of denying your reality, not just disagreeing with your opinion. If a colleague consistently tells you conversations did not happen, emails were never sent, or your recollection is always wrong despite evidence, that pattern suggests gaslighting.

faq.question: What should you do if you suspect a manager is gaslighting you?
faq.answer: Start documenting every interaction with dates and details. Save all emails and messages. Confide in a trusted colleague to verify your perception. If the pattern is clear, escalate to HR or a higher manager with documented evidence. Consider leaving if the organization enables it.
